379.title: Live with them in kindness
379.hook: live with your wives in kindness, even when you dislike something (4:19)
379.howItsDone: Muslims cite 4:19 and the hadith 'the best of you are the best to their families' in marriage sermons and counseling, as the basis for treating a spouse with recognized kindness and fairness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mirath: the shares, set out by name, after debts are paid. Your line was everyone has a share.

It's the dishes. Or the way they load the dishwasher. Or the phone at dinner, the late replies, the thing they always say at family gatherings. Share a home with someone long enough and a list can start. Most of the items are small. Some aren't. And the list can grow louder than everything else about the person. An-Nisa has a verse for exactly that moment, plain and practical.
screen: `IT'S THE DISHES.` → `A LIST STARTS.` → `THE LIST GETS LOUDER.`

segments.voice: Verse 19 starts by forbidding something commentators say was done in Arabia before Islam: when a man died, his heirs could treat his widow as part of the estate and control whom she married. The verse says no: it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will, and don't press them to give back what you gave them. Then it turns to marriage itself. In Pickthall's words: "But consort with them in kindness, for if ye hate them it may happen that ye hate a thing wherein Allah hath placed much good." The Arabic is 'ashiruhunna bil-ma'ruf. 'Ashara means to live together closely, as companions. Bil-ma'ruf: with the good everyone recognizes, the same ma'ruf as in calling to good. Not a special religious kindness, just the ordinary decency any neighbor would know. Then the surprise: if you dislike them, perhaps you dislike something in which God has placed much good. The verse expects dislike. It doesn't pretend a marriage is free of it. A hadith in Sahih Muslim puts it in household terms: a believing man should not hate a believing woman; if he dislikes one trait in her, he will be pleased with another. And a hadith in Tirmidhi reports the Prophet ﷺ saying: the best of you are the best to their families, and I am the best of you to my family. Some commentators apply the verse's principle to both spouses. The list is real. The verse simply asks you to keep reading past it, to the good on the other page.

Then find one good thing in them, something you'd miss if they were gone, then a second, until the complaint is no longer the only thing in the room.

380.title: Created weak
380.hook: Allah wants to lighten your burden, for humans were created weak (4:28)
380.tomorrow: The near neighbor and the far
380.howItsDone: Islamic law builds in concessions (rukhsa) for weakness, such as shortening prayers when traveling, praying seated when ill, and making up missed fasts, and Muslim teachers cite 4:28 and the hadith 'the religion is ease' when encouraging steady, moderate practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, 'ashara: live with them in kindness, even through dislike. Your line was kindness at home.

Some people open scripture expecting to be measured and found short: a list of rules, a standard nobody meets, a voice disappointed in them. Then, in the middle of family law in an-Nisa, after rules about whom you may marry and what to do if you can't afford it, the Qur'an pauses and says something about the reader that sounds almost tender. It explains why the rules are shaped the way they are. Because of what people are.
screen: `EXPECTING TO BE FOUND SHORT.` → `A PAUSE IN THE FAMILY LAW.` → `BECAUSE OF WHAT PEOPLE ARE.`

segments.voice: Read verses 26 to 28 together. God wants to make things clear to you, guide you in the ways of those before you, and turn to you in mercy, while those who follow their desires want you to swerve far off. Then 4:28, in Pickthall's words: "Allah would make the burden light for you, for man was created weak." Khuliqa al-insanu da'ifa. Da'if means weak, frail. Notice what the verse doesn't say. Not that people chose weakness, or that it's a failure. They were created that way. Weakness is part of the design, and the law is built around it. Commentators gave examples: weak in the face of desire, in patience, in body. In context, the marriage rules just before include allowances for people who can't manage the usual path. The Qur'an says something similar about fasting in 2:185: God wants ease for you, not hardship. And a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari reports the Prophet ﷺ saying the religion is ease, and no one makes it too hard for himself without being overwhelmed by it. So aim close to the mark, he said, and take heart. None of this means nothing is asked. The prayers are still prayed; the fast is still kept. But in the verse's picture, the asking comes from the One who knows the size of the one being asked. It echoes al-Baqarah's last verse: wus'a, not beyond what you can bear.
screen: `TO MAKE CLEAR, TO GUIDE, TO TURN` · `DA'IF: CREATED WEAK` · `THE LAW BUILT AROUND IT` · `THE RELIGION IS EASE` · then, large: `MAN WAS CREATED WEAK.`

segments.voice: Think of one place you've been hard on yourself lately: a habit not broken, a missed goal, a skipped prayer. Hear the voice you've been using, then try the verse's voice instead: you were made weak, and the load is meant to be light. Ask what a smaller, steadier, still faithful version of that goal would look like.

381.title: The near neighbor and the far
381.hook: kindness to parents, kin, orphans, the needy, neighbors near and far, travelers (4:36)
381.howItsDone: Muslims treat kindness to neighbors as a religious duty, whatever the neighbor's faith; many share food with neighbors at Eid and in Ramadan, following 4:36 and the hadith about Jibril's repeated urging.

segments.voice: Yesterday: created weak, and a burden made light. Your line was made weak, carried lightly.

Quick test. How many of your neighbors do you know by name? The people on either side, across the hall, across the street? Many people in big cities would answer one, maybe two. A podcast host's opinions can be better known than the name of the person whose kitchen shares your wall. An-Nisa has a verse that lists the people you owe kindness to, in widening circles, and neighbors appear on it twice.
screen: `HOW MANY NEIGHBORS BY NAME?` → `THE PERSON THROUGH THE WALL.` → `NEIGHBORS, LISTED TWICE.`

segments.voice: Verse 36 begins: worship God and associate nothing with Him. Then it moves straight to people, as if the two belong together. Be good to parents, relatives, orphans, the needy. To the neighbor who is near, and the neighbor who is far. To the companion at your side, the traveler, and those in your care. And it ends: God does not love the proud and the boastful. Al-jar dhi al-qurba, the near neighbor. Al-jar al-junub, the distant one, the stranger neighbor. Commentators read the pair in a few ways: a relative nearby and a neighbor who isn't related, or near in distance and farther down the road. Some early scholars said the far neighbor includes a neighbor of another faith. All the readings agree on one thing: being a neighbor creates a duty, whoever they are. The companion at your side, as-sahib bil-janb, is read as a fellow traveler, a coworker, a spouse: whoever happens to be next to you. The hadith collections press the point hard. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet ﷺ said the angel Jibril kept urging him to be good to the neighbor until he thought the neighbor would be made an heir. In another report, he said three times: by God, he does not believe. Asked who, he answered: the one whose neighbor is not safe from his harm. So the far neighbor isn't optional. The verse lists them right next to your parents.

382.title: Return the trusts
382.hook: return trusts to their owners and judge with justice (4:58)
382.howItsDone: Muslims treat amanah, trustworthiness, as a core trait of faith, covering loans, deposits, secrets, work and public office; the key of the Ka'bah is traditionally held by the Banu Shaybah, the family of Uthman ibn Talhah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-jar al-junub: the far neighbor, listed next to parents and kin. Your line was the far neighbor too.

Mecca, the day the Muslims entered the city after years of exile. The Prophet ﷺ goes to the Ka'bah, and the key to its door is brought to him from Uthman ibn Talhah, whose family kept it. Now the key is in the hand of the man who controls the city. Someone from his own family, his uncle al-Abbas in some reports, asks for the honor of holding it. Everyone is watching to see who gets the key.
screen: `MECCA, AFTER YEARS OF EXILE.` → `THE KEY TO THE KA'BAH.` → `WHO GETS THE KEY?`

segments.voice: Commentators report that he came out of the Ka'bah reciting 4:58. In Pickthall's words: "Lo! Allah commandeth you that ye restore deposits to their owners, and, if ye judge between mankind, that ye judge justly." And he gave the key back to Uthman ibn Talhah, saying it would stay with his family. Tradition says it has stayed with that family, the Banu Shaybah, ever since. The Arabic for deposits is amanat, trusts: anything placed in your care. The root is the same as iman, faith, and amn, safety. A trust is a small piece of safety someone hands you. This wasn't new for the Prophet. The sira says that before his prophethood, Meccans called him al-Amin, the trustworthy, and left their valuables with him, and kept doing it even when they turned against him. On the night he left Mecca for Medina, with enemies at his door, the sira reports he left Ali behind to return every deposit to its owner. Scholars read the verse widely: a loan, a secret, a borrowed book, a job you were hired to do, a public office. The second half, judge justly, they read as a trust too: power over others is placed in your hands for a while, and owed back. A hadith in Bukhari lists among the signs of a hypocrite: when trusted, he betrays. A key, a lent jacket, a secret, a job. Whatever was put in your hands for a while, give it back whole.

Amanah, a trust, anything placed in your care. Restore the amanat to their owners, and judge justly, from 4:58: the verse recited with the key to the Ka'bah. Today's word.

383.title: Refer it back
383.hook: in a dispute, refer it to Allah and the messenger (4:59)
383.carry: make it about what, not who
383.howItsDone: Muslims resolve questions of religious practice by referring them to the Qur'an and the Sunnah, through scholars and the schools of law; 4:59 is a foundation of Islamic legal reasoning and of the principle that obedience to authority is limited to what is right.

segments.voice: Yesterday, amanah: the key to the Ka'bah, handed back. Your line was give it back.

Two siblings are arguing about how to care for an aging parent. One wants to move her in; one wants a care home. It's been weeks, and each conversation ends in the same place, louder. Neither is wrong to care. The trouble is they keep arguing about who's right, instead of asking what they both already agree should decide it. The verse right after yesterday's gives a method for exactly that kind of stuck.
screen: `TWO SIBLINGS, ONE PARENT.` → `WEEKS OF THE SAME ARGUMENT.` → `WHAT SHOULD DECIDE IT?`

segments.voice: Verse 59 opens: O you who believe, obey God, and obey the messenger, and those in authority among you. Then, in Pickthall's words: "and if ye have a dispute concerning any matter, refer it to Allah and the messenger." That, the verse says, is better, and more fitting in the end. Look at the grammar. Obey is said before God, and again before the messenger, but not before those in authority, ulu al-amr. Some commentators drew a lesson from that: obedience to people in charge is tied to obedience to God, not free-standing. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari makes it vivid. A commander, angry with his troops, ordered them to build a fire and walk into it. They refused. When the Prophet ﷺ heard, he said if they had entered it they would never have come out; obedience is only in what is right. Who are those in authority? Sunni scholars give different answers: rulers and commanders, or the learned, or both. Shia Muslims understand them as the Imams of the Prophet's family. And after the Prophet's death, refer it to God and the messenger is commonly read as: to the Qur'an and to his Sunnah, his example. So the verse doesn't say the loudest wins, or whoever's in charge wins. When you disagree, step back from the two of you and take the question to a source you both already accept. For the siblings, that might be the Qur'an's command to honor parents, or simply what their mother herself wants. Disputes stay stuck when they're about who. They move when they're about what.
screen: `OBEY, OBEY, AND THOSE IN AUTHORITY` · `THE FIRE THEY REFUSED TO ENTER` · `THE QUR'AN AND THE SUNNAH` · `NOT WHO, BUT WHAT` · then, large: `REFER IT TO ALLAH AND THE MESSENGER.`

Ulu al-amr, those in authority. Obedience to them is tied to obedience to God, not free-standing, from 4:59.
Your line: make it about what, not who. A shared source can settle what two loud voices can't. Day three hundred eighty-three, done.

384.title: Greet with better
384.hook: when greeted, return a better greeting or the same (4:86)
384.carry: add the mercy and the blessings
384.howItsDone: Muslims greet each other with as-salamu 'alaykum and are taught to return it with at least the same, and ideally more: wa 'alaykum as-salam wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ulu al-amr: in a dispute, refer it back to a source above both sides. Your line was make it about what, not who.

Someone texts you: good morning! You reply: morning. Someone at work says: hope your weekend was great. You say: yep, you too. Nothing wrong with it. Now picture a reply with a little more than you were given: a name, a question, a real wish. It lands differently. An-Nisa, between laws about war and peace, stops to give a rule about something as small as hello.
screen: `GOOD MORNING! → MORNING.` → `A LITTLE MORE THAN YOU GAVE.` → `A RULE ABOUT HELLO.`

segments.voice: Here's 4:86 in Pickthall's words: "When ye are greeted with a greeting, greet ye with a better than it or return it. Lo! Allah taketh count of all things." The word for greeting is tahiyyah, from the root of hayah, life: at its root, a greeting is a wish for someone's life. The rule has two levels. The minimum: give back what you were given. The better way: add to it. The Muslim greeting shows how. As-salamu 'alaykum: peace be upon you. The better reply adds a layer: wa 'alaykum as-salam wa rahmatullah, and upon you be peace, and God's mercy. Better still: wa barakatuh, and His blessings. A hadith in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi tells it. A man said as-salamu 'alaykum, and the Prophet ﷺ answered him and said: ten. Another added wa rahmatullah: twenty. A third added wa barakatuh: thirty. Commentators explain: ten good deeds for each piece. And a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari takes the custom back to the beginning. When God created Adam, He told him to go and greet a group of angels and listen to their answer, because it would be the greeting of his children. Adam said as-salamu 'alaykum. The angels replied: as-salamu 'alayka wa rahmatullah. They added mercy. In the story, the first greeting is answered with better. And the verse's last line: God takes count of all things. In the verse, even a hello is counted.

385.title: Justice against yourselves
385.hook: stand firm for justice even against yourselves, parents or kin (4:135)
385.tomorrow: Peace between the two is better
385.howItsDone: Muslims hold 'adl, justice, as a central duty, and 4:135 is quoted by judges, scholars and activists to insist that testimony and judgment must be honest even against oneself and one's family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tahiyyah: greet with better, like the angels who added mercy to Adam's hello. Your line was add the mercy and the blessings.

It's easy to be fair about strangers. It's harder about your brother. When your own kid is in the playground fight, when your parent cut in line, when your company fudged the numbers, the mind gets very creative very fast. Suddenly there's context. There were reasons. The other side started it. An-Nisa has a verse that goes straight for that blind spot and names it out loud.
screen: `FAIR ABOUT STRANGERS.` → `HARDER ABOUT YOUR BROTHER.` → `SUDDENLY THERE'S CONTEXT.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's words, 4:135 says: "O ye who believe! Be ye staunch in justice, witnesses for Allah, even though it be against yourselves or (your) parents or (your) kindred." Rich or poor, the verse goes on, God is nearer to both than you are. So don't follow your desires and swerve from justice. The Arabic for staunch, qawwamin, is an intensive form: not people who are fair once, but people who keep standing up for justice, again and again. And at the end, the verb ta'dilu, from 'adl, justice: being level, like two pans of a scale at rest. Look at the order. Yourselves first. Then parents, whom the Qur'an elsewhere tells people to honor. Then relatives. Honoring your parents, the verse implies, never means lying for them. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari shows the Prophet ﷺ holding to this. A woman from a powerful Meccan clan was caught stealing, and her family sent someone the Prophet loved to ask for her to be let off. He was angry, and said peoples before them had been ruined because they let the powerful go and punished the weak. Then he named his own family: even if it were Fatimah, his own daughter, the law would be the same. So this week ends where it began: kindness at home, burdens carried lightly, the near neighbor and the far, trusts returned, disputes referred back, greetings answered with better. And now the one that turns the mirror around: justice that starts with me.
screen: `QAWWAMIN: STANDING UP, AGAIN AND AGAIN` · `YOURSELVES FIRST, THEN PARENTS` · `'ADL: THE SCALE AT REST` · `EVEN IF IT WERE FATIMAH` · then, large: `EVEN THOUGH IT BE AGAINST YOURSELVES.`

segments.voice: Think of a recent conflict where you were part of the problem, maybe not the whole problem, but part. Picture it as an honest witness would, without defending yourself, and find one plain sentence of admission: I was unfair about that. I see it now.
'Adl. Justice: being level, like a balanced scale, even against yourself, your parents or your kin, from 4:135. Today's word.
Your line: justice, even against me. Yourselves first, then parents, then kin. And that's a week.
